title: Measure the rain, survive the heat, prove your savings

say: Measure the rain, survive the heat, prove your savings.
This is the video for module two of Climate Awareness and Community Resilience.
Memories show the big picture. A daily log shows exactly what is happening this season, in the unit weather services use.

say: You will also learn to protect the people most at risk from heat, and to measure whether your household actions really work.

say: Use a clear jar with straight sides and a flat bottom. Hold a ruler upright from the inside bottom and read the depth in millimetres. The width does not matter, as long as the sides are straight.

panel.heading: Build, place and read your gauge
items: Straight-sided clear jar, at least 10 cm wide
Open place, away from roofs, walls and trees
Fix it firmly, top about 30 cm above ground
Read at the same time every morning
Write 0 on dry days

say: Keep it at least as far from any obstacle as that obstacle is tall.

say: Tie it to a short post or set it in a tin of sand, so wind, goats or children cannot knock it over.

say: Read it at the same time each morning, for example 7 am. On dry days, write zero. A zero is a reading too.

say: At the end of each month, work out three numbers. Hadiza in Minna added all her June readings: 100.5 millimetres.

panel.heading: Hadiza's June in three numbers
items: Total rain: 100.5 mm
Rainy days of 1 mm or more: 8
Longest dry run: 7 days
Action: mulch and water in long dry runs

say: She counted rainy days, only days with 1 millimetre or more. That gave 8.

items: Total rain: 100.5 mm

say: Heat is quieter than floods, but it is dangerous. Older people, especially over 65, feel thirst and heat less well.

panel.heading: Who is most at risk from heat
items: Older people, especially over 65
Babies, young children and pregnant women
People with long-term illness or disability
Outdoor workers: farmers, traders, okada riders
Families in hot, crowded rooms

say: Babies heat up quickly. Pregnant women, people with long-term illness, and people who cannot move to a cooler place alone are also at higher risk.

say: So are outdoor workers, and families in rooms with metal roofs and one small window.
WHO advises avoiding hard work in the hottest time of day, and drinking water regularly, about 2 to 3 litres a day, before you feel thirsty.

say: Heat exhaustion looks like tiredness, dizziness, headache and heavy sweating. Move the person to a cool, shady place, give water to sip, and sponge and fan the skin. If they are not better within about 30 minutes, treat it as heatstroke.

panel.heading: Know the danger signs

cards.d: Dizzy, headache, heavy sweating. Move to shade, give sips of water, sponge and fan.
Hot skin, confusion, fits, collapse. Get help at once or call 112. Cool with water and fan.
Lay them on their side, keep checking breathing. No drinks if not fully awake.

say: Heatstroke is a medical emergency. Signs include hot skin, confusion, fits or collapse. Get emergency help at once, or call 112, and keep cooling them while you wait.

panel.heading: Know the danger signs

cards.d: Dizzy, headache, heavy sweating. Move to shade, give sips of water, sponge and fan.
Hot skin, confusion, fits, collapse. Get help at once or call 112. Cool with water and fan.
Lay them on their side, keep checking breathing. No drinks if not fully awake.

say: If the person becomes unconscious, lay them on their side and keep checking their breathing. Never give drinks to someone who is not fully awake, and never give medicines without a health worker's advice.

say: Close curtains or hang a damp cloth on the sunny side by day, and let air flow through at night. Cook outside, and let an older relative or a baby sleep in the coolest room.

panel.heading: Keep the home cool and safe
left: Coolest room for the most at risk
right: Put a generator near a window or door
Bring a glowing charcoal stove inside

say: Never run a generator indoors, on a closed veranda, or near a window or door. And never bring a glowing charcoal stove into a closed room. Both give off carbon monoxide, a gas you cannot see or smell, which can kill sleeping people.

say: Funke weighed her charcoal for four weeks first. That is her baseline: 9 kg a week on average.
Then she made one change. A lid on every pot, and a retained-heat basket, where a boiling pot keeps cooking in a box packed with cloths. Four weeks later, she used 6.75 kg a week.

card.title: Did Funke's basket save charcoal?

say: She pays about 700 naira per kg, though prices vary.

say: She saves 2.25 kg a week. That is 25% less charcoal, and about 1,575 naira a week.

say: Over 52 weeks, that is about 81,900 naira. She is saving the difference towards a gas cooker.
Measure a baseline first, change one thing at a time, and compare ordinary weeks with ordinary weeks.

say: To remember. Read your gauge every day and record zeros. Sum up each month in three numbers. Treat heatstroke as an emergency. Never run a generator or charcoal stove indoors. And measure a baseline before you change anything.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Read the gauge daily, record zeros, empty it
Monthly: total rain, rainy days, longest dry run
Heatstroke is an emergency: get help, call 112
Never run a generator or charcoal stove indoors
Baseline first, one change, then measure again

say: Now build your gauge and log a week. Post the danger signs where everyone can see them, agree check-ins with high-risk neighbours, with their permission, and record your baseline.
